tools.name: pipe__get
tools.description: Read the arguments or the result of an earlier tool call by its handle. Handle forms: "c3.out" (result), "c3.in" (arguments); add a path to read part of a value, e.g. "c3.out.items[0].id". Optional "jq" applies a jq filter to the value first. "status" returns the connected servers and any startup errors.

handle.description: call handle with optional path, or "status"

jq.description: optional jq filter applied to the value

tools.name: pipe__patch
tools.description: Re-run an earlier tool call with modified arguments, sending only the change. The call's stored arguments are copied, the edits are applied to the copy, and the result is executed as a new call with its own handle. Edit forms: {find, replace} replaces text in string arguments (all of them, or only under "path"); {path, set} sets the value at "path". With no edits the call is re-run unchanged. To fix a step of a run instead, pass "run" (run id) and "step": the edits apply to the step definition (e.g. path "args.sql", or find/replace in its text) and the run continues from that step; earlier steps are not repeated.

run.description: run id (with "step"); or, with "call", false to only store the new call

path.description: path inside the arguments / step, e.g. "a.b[0]"

rerun.description: with run+step: continue the run after patching (default true)

tools.name: pipe__transform
tools.description: Reshape a stored value with a jq filter and store the output under a new handle, without the data passing through the conversation. "from" is a handle with optional path (e.g. "c3.out.items").

from.description: handle of the input value, e.g. "c3.out"

tools.name: pipe__map
tools.description: Call one tool once per item of a stored list, in a single request. "over" is a handle of a list (e.g. "c3.out.rows", or "{{ c3.out | map(.id) }}"). In "args", "{{ item }}" is the current item and "{{ item.<path> }}" part of it. Returns how many calls succeeded, the failures, and a handle per call; the outputs are stored as a list under the map's own handle. "dry_run" returns the plan only.

over.description: handle of the list to iterate

args.description: arguments for each call; may use {{ item }} refs

confirm.description: only if a reply asked for it: the token from that needs_confirm reply

tools.name: pipe__run
tools.description: Run a multi-step plan in one request: pass a new "chain" (JSON or YAML text, e.g. copied from a skill) with its "params", or an existing "run" id to run it again. Steps run back to back in one request; every step's output is saved and can be referred to by later steps. A chain is {params?: {name: type}, steps: [...]}; each step has an "id" and one of: {call: "<tool>", args: {...}} calls a tool; {jq: "<program>"} computes a value, with params and earlier step outputs as jq variables ($id); {map: "<tool>", over: "<step id or handle of a list>", args: {...}} calls a tool once per item ("{{ item }}", "{{ item.path }}"); {ai: "<task>", input?: "<jq program>", by?: "session"|"subagent", batch?: n, expect?: <JSON Schema>} pauses the run for a step that needs judgement (done by you or a subagent), continued with pipe__resume. In args, "{{ name[.path] [| jq] }}" refers to a param, an earlier step's output, or any handle. The reply lists each step's output handle and the last step's result. A failing step stops the run; pipe__patch {run, step, edits} edits that step and re-runs from it without repeating earlier ones. "from" re-runs from a step; "dry_run" returns the plan; "force" repeats map items that already succeeded.

from.description: step id to run again from

dry_run.description: validate and return the plan without running it

confirm.description: only if a reply asked for it: the token from that needs_confirm reply

tools.name: pipe__resume
tools.description: Give the result of a paused ai step and continue its run. "output" is checked against the step's "expect"; if it does not match, the reply says why and the run stays paused. For a batched step, resume each chunk by its index.

<skill name="skills/mcp-pipe/SKILL.md">
---
name: mcp-pipe
description: How to work with tools served through mcp-pipe (tools named <server>__<tool> plus pipe__run, pipe__patch, pipe__transform, pipe__map, pipe__get, pipe__resume). Use for any task that calls these tools, especially when data from one tool goes into another, a list needs one call per item, or a call has to be fixed and repeated.
---

# Working with mcp-pipe

mcp-pipe sits between you and the MCP servers. It saves every call: its arguments and its result. Each result ends with its reference, for example `saved as {{ c7.out }}`. Work with these references instead of with the data itself.

## Rules

1. **Never copy data from a result into another call.** Pass the reference instead. mcp-pipe fills in the value before the call:
   - the whole result: `"{{ c7.out }}"`
   - a part: `"{{ c7.out.rows[0].id }}"`
   - reshaped with jq: `"{{ c7.out | map([.name, .total]) }}"`
   - any jq expression over saved results: `"{{ [["Name", "Total"]] + (c7.out | map([.name, .total])) }}"`

   A string that is exactly one reference becomes the value with its own type (array, object, number). A reference inside longer text is inserted as text.
2. **Compute in the tools, not in your head.** Percentages, totals, rounding, formatting and joins belong in the query (SQL) or in jq over a saved result. Write the formula, not the numbers.
3. **Fix a call by patching it, not by rewriting it.** `pipe__patch {"call": "c3", "edits": [{"find": "usr_id", "replace": "user_id"}]}` copies the saved arguments, applies the change and runs the call again. Edits are `{find, replace}` (text in string arguments) or `{path, set}` (any value).
4. **Read only what you need.** Large results come back as a preview. Use `pipe__get {"handle": "c7.out.rows", "jq": ".[0:5]"}` or a path like `c7.out.rows[0].id` for the part you need, not the whole value.
5. **`pipe__transform` must transform its input.** It applies jq to a saved value and saves the result under a new reference. A filter that ignores its input is refused; pass literal values directly in the tool argument instead.

## Workflow

1. **Look first, with single calls.** Read schemas and descriptions, take small samples (`LIMIT 3`), check date ranges and IDs. Don't trust metadata blindly: if a call fails on a name from the docs, check the real one, then patch.
2. **Then write the rest as one pipe** and run it with `pipe__run`. Do this as soon as you know the remaining steps, especially when one step's output feeds the next. The steps run back to back without a round trip through you, and no intermediate data enters the conversation.
3. **If a step fails, patch that step.** `pipe__patch {"run": "r1", "step": "cohorts", "edits": [...]}` edits the step and continues the run from it. Earlier steps are not repeated. Don't write a new pipe.
4. **Report from the outputs.** The reply lists each step's reference and the last step's result. Use `pipe__get` on a step output if you need to show part of it.

Single calls are fine for one-off lookups. Use a pipe once there are two or more dependent steps.

## Pipe format

`pipe__run {"chain": <YAML or JSON>, "params": {...}}`:

```yaml
params: { sql: string, channel: string }
steps:
  - id: rows                      # a tool call
    call: db__run_query
    args: { sql: "{{ sql }}" }
  - id: table                     # jq: params and earlier steps are $variables
    jq: '[["Country", "Revenue"]] + ($rows | map([.country, .revenue]))'
  - id: sheet
    call: sheets__create_spreadsheet
    args: { title: "Revenue" }
  - id: write                     # earlier steps as references in arguments
    call: sheets__update_values
    args: { spreadsheet_id: "{{ sheet.spreadsheet_id }}", start_cell: "A1", values: "{{ table }}" }
  - id: notify                    # one call per item of a list
    map: chat__post_message
    over: rows
    args: { channel: "{{ channel }}", text: "{{ item.country }}: {{ item.revenue }}" }
```

- In `args`, `{{ name }}` refers to a param, an earlier step id, or any saved call (`c7.out`). In `jq`, they are `$name`.
- `map` steps call a tool once per item: `{{ item }}`, `{{ item.path }}`. Items that already succeeded are skipped when the step runs again.
- `dry_run: true` checks the pipe and returns the plan without running it. `from: "<step>"` runs again from a step.

### Steps that need judgement

An `ai` step pauses the run for work only a model can do (translate, classify, summarise):

```yaml
  - id: tr
    ai: "Translate each item to Hebrew. Return a JSON array, same order, same length."
    input: '$boxes | map(.text)'
    by: subagent                  # or session
    batch: 20
    expect: { type: array, items: { type: string }, sameLengthAs: boxes }
```

The reply has `status: "paused"`, the `task`, and the input (inline for `by: session`, or as `inputHandle` per chunk for `by: subagent`).
- **`by: session`:** do the task on the input yourself, then call `pipe__resume {"run", "step", "output"}`.
- **`by: subagent`:** start one subagent per open chunk. Each one reads its input with `pipe__get {"handle": "<inputHandle>"}`, does the task and calls `pipe__resume {"run", "step", "chunk", "output"}`. Don't read the input yourself.

`output` is checked against `expect`. If it doesn't match, the reply says why and the run stays paused.

## Reusing a pipe

mcp-pipe stores no named workflows. When the user wants to keep a pipe that worked, write it into a skill: a short description of when to use it, the params, and the YAML. Next time, read the skill, change tool or column names if they differ, and pass the YAML to `pipe__run`.

## Per-item work outside a pipe

`pipe__map {"tool": "crm__update", "over": "c5.out", "args": {"id": "{{ item.id }}"}}` calls a tool once per item of a saved list in one request, and returns the counts, failures and one reference per call.
</skill>

content.text: Metadata says `usr_id` but the column doesn't exist; let me check the real columns.

input.sql:
WITH u AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(signup_date) AS signup_date FROM users_data
  WHERE signup_date BETWEEN '2026-07-01' AND '2026-09-30' GROUP BY user_id
), a AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT e.user_id, CAST(julianday(date(e.event_time)) - julianday(u.signup_date) AS INTEGER) AS d
  FROM users_data e JOIN u ON u.user_id = e.user_id
), f AS (
  SELECT u.user_id, strftime('%Y-%m', u.signup_date) AS cohort,
    MAX(a.d BETWEEN 1 AND 7) AS w1, MAX(a.d BETWEEN 8 AND 14) AS w2, MAX(a.d BETWEEN 15 AND 30) AS m1, MAX(a.d BETWEEN 1 AND 30) AS any30
  FROM u LEFT JOIN a ON a.user_id = u.user_id GROUP BY u.user_id, cohort
)
SELECT cohort, COUNT(*) AS users,
  ROUND(100.0*SUM(COALESCE(w1,0))/COUNT(*),1) AS d1_7_pct,
  ROUND(100.0*SUM(COALESCE(w2,0))/COUNT(*),1) AS d8_14_pct,
  ROUND(100.0*SUM(COALESCE(m1,0))/COUNT(*),1) AS d15_30_pct,
  ROUND(100.0*SUM(COALESCE(any30,0))/COUNT(*),1) AS d1_30_pct
FROM f GROUP BY cohort
UNION ALL
SELECT 'Q3 2026 total', COUNT(*),
  ROUND(100.0*SUM(COALESCE(w1,0))/COUNT(*),1), ROUND(100.0*SUM(COALESCE(w2,0))/COUNT(*),1),
  ROUND(100.0*SUM(COALESCE(m1,0))/COUNT(*),1), ROUND(100.0*SUM(COALESCE(any30,0))/COUNT(*),1)
FROM f

content.text:
I calculated retention for users who signed up in Q3 2026 (July–September), saved the results to a new spreadsheet and posted a summary with the link to #analytics.

**Spreadsheet:** https://sheets.example.com/sh1

**Q3 2026: 354 new users**

| Signup month | Users | Days 1–7 | Days 8–14 | Days 15–30 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jul | 121 | 97.5% | 62.8% | 69.4% |
| Aug | 118 | 97.5% | 61.9% | 70.3% |
| Sep | 115 | 98.3% | 60.9% | 67.0% |
| **Total** | **354** | **97.7%** | **61.9%** | **68.9%** |

- **Main finding:** almost everyone comes back in the first week, then about 4 in 10 users drop off in the second week. The three months are very close to each other.
- **Days 15–30 is higher than days 8–14,** but only because that window is longer (16 days vs 7). It doesn't mean users are coming back.

**How I calculated it:**
- **"Last quarter":** the data runs to 11 Nov 2026, so I used Q3 2026, the last complete quarter. Every Q3 signup has had at least 30 days to show up in the data.
- **Retained:** a user counts as retained in a window if they had any event (login, page view or purchase) in that period after signup.
- **Column name:** the table's documentation says `usr_id`, but the real column is `user_id`, so the query uses that.

**Worth checking:** 100% of users had at least one event in their first 30 days, which is unusually high. It could mean the data only includes active users, or that it's test data. I'd check that before relying on these numbers.
